tip: -아/어서 glues 'because' straight onto the verb: 비슷해서 (biseuthaeseo) = because they're similar – cause first, result after, no separate word for 'because'.
Adding 주다 (juda = give) after a verb marks it as done for someone's benefit: 지켜 줬어요 (jikyeo jwosseoyo) = kept it as a favor to my friend, not just kept it.
-든지 turns question words into any-words: 뭐든지 (mwodeunji) = anything, 누구든지 (nugudeunji) = anyone, 언제든지 (eonjedeunji) = anytime. One suffix, a whole series.
You don't 'have' a chat in Korean – you shake one: 수다를 떨다 (suda-reul tteolda), where 떨다 (tteolda) means shake or rattle. 떨었어요 (tteoreosseoyo) = chattered away.
말이 통해요 (mari tonghaeyo) is literally 'words get through' – 통하다 (tonghada) means to flow or pass through. Clicking with someone = your words flow freely.
첫눈에 반했어요 (cheonnune banhaesseoyo) = fell for them 'at first eye': 첫눈 (cheonnun) is literally 'first eye/glance'. Same idea as English's first sight, built from the eye.
시작하다 (sijakhada = start) needs a noun, so -기 turns the verb into one: 사귀기 시작했어요 (sagwigi sijakhaesseoyo) = started dating, literally 'started the dating'.
좋아하다 (joahada) is a true verb, so you can say it about anyone: 그는 좋아해요 (geuneun joahaeyo) = he likes. Plain feeling adjectives can't describe a third person that directly.
긴장됐어요 (ginjangdwaesseoyo) is built on 되다 (doeda = become): nerves are something that happens to you in Korean, not a state you are.
Korean splits phoning: 전화하다 (jeonhwahada) = place the call, 통화하다 (tonghwahada) = have the conversation. Nightly 통화해요 (tonghwahaeyo) means real talks, not dialing.
In 생각이 나요 (saenggagi nayo) the thought is the subject: it 'comes up' on its own – 나다 (nada) = arise. You're not doing the thinking; the person keeps surfacing in your head.
-지 못하다 is the long form of 못 (mot = can't): 고백하지 못했어요 (gobaekhaji mothaesseoyo) = haven't been able to confess – inability, not just 'didn't'.
-(으)면 covers both 'if' and 'when' in one ending: 사귀면 (sagwimyeon) = if/once you date. English forces a choice between the two; Korean leaves it to context.
-보다 (boda = than) attaches straight to the thing compared: 연애보다 (yeonaeboda) = than dating. The order flips English: 'than dating, work is more important'.
-고 chains actions and only the last verb takes the tense: 잡고 걸었어요 (japgo georeosseoyo) = held and walked – 잡고 stays bare, 걸었어요 carries the past for both.
께서 (kkeseo) is the respect version of the subject marker, and the verb matches with -시-: 어머니께서 나셨어요 (eomeonikkeseo nasyeosseoyo). Respect is marked twice – noun and verb.
한테 (hante = to) upgrades to 께 (kke) when the receiver is respected: 부모님께 (bumonimkke) = to my parents. The particle alone signals the respect, before the verb does.
사과할게요 (sagwahalgeyo) is not plain future: -(으)ㄹ게요 makes it a promise to the listener – 'I'll apologize, count on it'. It only works with someone there to hear it.
다시는 (dasineun) with a negative means 'never again': 하지 않을게요 (haji aneulgeyo) = I promise not to do it – together, a never-again promise with the 'ever' built in.
주다 (juda) marks a favor; it becomes 주시다 (jusida) when the favor-doer is honored: 이해해 주셨어요 (ihaehae jusyeosseoyo) = she kindly understood – respect for mom built into the verb.
Inner feelings need -어하다 when said of others, but looks are visible to all, so 아름답다 (areumdapda) stays plain: 아름다웠어요 (areumdawosseoyo) = she was beautiful.
In a guess the tense lives on 같다 (gatda = seem): 긴장한 것 같았어요 (ginjanghan geot gatasseoyo) = it seemed he was nervous – 같았어요 is past because the seeming was then.
행복하시길 바라요 (haengbokhasigil barayo): the -시- inside honors the couple being wished well, while plain 바라요 (barayo = I hope) is your own act – no honoring yourself.
Verbs sit in front of nouns like adjectives: 좋아하는 가수 (joahaneun gasu) = 'the liking singer', i.e. the singer I like. English puts the clause after; Korean packs it before, with -는.
만에 after a time span = 'in only that long': 십 분 만에 (sip bun mane) = in just ten minutes. It carries the surprise at the speed – the tickets vanished that fast.
-자마자 means 'as soon as' with zero gap: 나오자마자 (naojamaja) = the instant it came out. The two actions touch – no time allowed between release and purchase.
'And' between nouns picks its shape by sound: 와 (wa) after vowels, 과 (gwa) after consonants. 춤 (chum) ends in a consonant, so it's 춤과 노래 (chumgwa norae) = dance and song.
세 곡이나 (se gogina) isn't just 'three songs' – the -이나 adds surprise at the amount: 'three whole songs!'. Drop it and the number turns neutral.
여운이 남았어요 (yeouni namasseoyo): 여운 is literally the lingering sound after a note ends, and 남다 (namda) = remain. Korean says the concert's echo stayed behind.
-부터 (buteo) marks the starting point: 데뷔 때부터 (debwi ttaebuteo) = from the time of their debut. 때 (ttae = time) plus -부터 builds 'ever since' for any event.
Reported 'let's' has its own ending: -자고 하다. 가자고 했어요 (gajago haesseoyo) = said 'let's go' – the 자 (ja) carries the suggestion, so no quotation marks needed.
Korean location words are nouns: 무대 위 (mudae wi) = 'the stage's top'. With -의 (ui) it modifies the next noun: 무대 위의 가수 (mudae wiui gasu) = the on-stage singer.
방 (bang = room) builds venues: 노래방 (noraebang) = song-room, i.e. karaoke. The same pattern gives PC방 (PC-bang, internet cafe) and 찜질방 (jjimjilbang, sauna).
를 위해 (reul wihae) = 'for the sake of': 가수를 위해 (gasureul wihae) = for their singer. It marks who benefits – stronger and more deliberate than plain 'for'.
Purpose of movement gets its own ending: 보러 갔어요 (boreo gasseoyo) = went in order to watch. -(으)러 only attaches to going/coming verbs – it states why you moved.
바탕 (batang) = base or foundation: 실화를 바탕으로 (silhwareul batangeuro) = 'with a true story as the base'. That's how Korean says 'based on' – the source is the ground under it.
You don't 'be popular' in Korean – you have lots of popularity: 인기가 많아요 (ingiga manayo), literally 'popularity is plentiful'. Popularity is a possession, not a trait.
사서 먹었어요 (saseo meogeosseoyo) = bought it and ate that very popcorn – -아/어서 keeps the first action's result in hand. Plain -고 would just list two separate acts.
몰다 (molda) = to herd or drive together: 몰아서 봤어요 (moraseo bwasseoyo) = watched them herded into one sitting. Korean binge-watching literally rounds the episodes up.
-적인 turns idea-nouns into adjectives: 감동 (gamdong = deep emotion) grows into 감동적인 (gamdongjeogin) = moving. One suffix, hundreds of instant adjectives.
없이 (eopsi) after a noun = 'without it': 자막 없이 (jamak eopsi) = without subtitles. It's the adverb form of 없다 (eopda = to not exist) – 'the subtitles not existing'.
원작 (wonjak) = the original work: 소설을 원작으로 해요 (soseoreul wonjageuro haeyo) = takes the novel as its original. This is the set pattern for calling something an adaptation.
-고도 = 'even after / even just': 예고편만 보고도 (yegopyeonman bogodo) = even just from watching the trailer. It flags a result arriving earlier than expected – tears before the film.
'Must not' is built from 'if': 찍으면 안 돼요 (jjigeumyeon an dwaeyo) is literally 'if you photograph, it won't do'. Korean bans things by condition, not command.
-아/어야 means 'only if': 예약을 해야 볼 수 있어요 (yeyageul haeya bol su isseoyo) = only if you reserve can you see it. The condition ending itself carries the 'only'.
